items.title: I can define attention and explain its general purpose
items.what: Attention is the process of actively focusing on particular information while simultaneously ignoring other information. It allows us to direct limited mental resources toward the most relevant stimuli.
items.why: Without attention, we would be overwhelmed by every stimulus in our environment and unable to complete tasks or respond meaningfully to the world.
items.example: A student in a noisy cafeteria focuses on reading their notes before an exam, tuning out surrounding conversations.

subtopic.name: Types of Attention
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of attention and the three main types: sustained, divided, and selective. It also distinguishes between internal and external stimuli as the two sources of information that attention can be directed toward.
subtopic.why: Understanding the different types of attention helps explain why we can concentrate on some tasks but not others, and why multitasking often reduces performance. These concepts underpin much of how humans navigate complex environments.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external stimuli
items.what: Internal stimuli originate from within the body, such as hunger, pain, or a thought. External stimuli originate from outside the body, such as a conversation, a sound, or something seen.
items.why: Both types of stimuli compete for our attention at all times, so identifying their source helps explain why attention can be disrupted by things as varied as a headache or a loud noise.
items.example: While writing an essay, a student is distracted by both a headache (internal stimulus) and music playing nearby (external stimulus).

items.title: I can define sustained attention and describe its three stages
items.what: Sustained attention is the ability to focus on one stimulus or task across a prolonged, continuous period of time. It involves three stages: focusing attention on the stimulus, maintaining that attention, and then releasing it when no longer needed.
items.why: Many daily tasks require sustained attention to be completed accurately, and understanding its stages helps explain when and why attention breaks down.
items.example: A student completing a 45-minute exam paper must focus on each question, maintain attention across the full period, and release it when they hand in their paper.

items.title: I can explain the effect of distraction on sustained attention
items.what: Distractions are internal or external stimuli that draw attention away from the current task. They force an individual to repeatedly refocus, which reduces the effectiveness of sustained attention, particularly when the task is boring or when the person is fatigued.
items.why: Recognising how distraction impairs sustained attention explains why study environments and task engagement matter for cognitive performance.
items.example: A student trying to memorise notes while their phone keeps buzzing must refocus repeatedly, making the study session less efficient than one without interruptions.

items.title: I can define divided attention and identify when it is used
items.what: Divided attention involves splitting attention across two or more stimuli or tasks at the same time, which is the basis of multitasking. It tends to be more successful when at least one of the tasks is automatic or easy.
items.why: Divided attention is common in everyday life, but understanding its limits helps explain why performance on complex tasks decreases when we try to do multiple things at once.
items.example: A student takes notes from the board while simultaneously listening to the teacher explain a concept, dividing attention between two related tasks.

items.title: I can explain the negative implications of multitasking on performance
items.what: Multitasking can reduce performance when tasks are complex, unrelated, or use different platforms or mediums. Switching between tasks increases distractibility and reduces depth of understanding.
items.why: People often overestimate their multitasking ability; understanding its costs supports better decisions about how to allocate attention during study or work.
items.example: Writing an essay while online shopping results in slower writing, less coherent arguments, and missed ideas because both tasks compete for limited attentional resources.

items.title: I can define selective attention and provide examples of it in action
items.what: Selective attention involves exclusively focusing on one specific stimulus or task while ignoring all others, acting as a filter on both external stimuli (other sounds, sights) and internal stimuli (thoughts, emotions).
items.why: Selective attention is essential for prioritising what is most relevant in complex or busy environments where many stimuli are present simultaneously.
items.example: At a crowded party, a person focuses entirely on the conversation they are having, filtering out the many other voices and music in the room.

items.title: I can explain the role of sustained attention in making sense of the world
items.what: Sustained attention allows us to process incoming information in sufficient detail by spending the necessary time and mental energy on it. Without it, we cannot adapt to environmental changes or fully complete cognitive tasks.
items.why: Many real-world tasks, from solving a maths problem to following a lecture, require enough sustained attention to process all relevant information before shifting focus.
items.example: A student needs several minutes of sustained attention to work through a multi-step physics problem; if they look away after 15 seconds, they cannot complete the calculation.

subtopic.name: Attention and Making Sense of the World
subtopic.what: This subtopic explains the specific roles that sustained, divided, and selective attention each play in how humans process and make sense of their internal and external environments. It also introduces the two principles of attentional allocation that guide selective attention.
subtopic.why: Understanding how each type of attention serves a different function helps explain real-world behaviours like noticing a familiar name in a crowd, losing track of a task when fatigued, or being able to drive and hold a conversation.

items.title: I can explain the role of divided attention in making sense of the world
items.what: Divided attention allows us to understand and respond to multiple aspects of our environment at once, which is necessary given how many events occur simultaneously around us. However, it is limited by how many things the brain can process at one time.
items.why: In dynamic environments, being able to process multiple inputs simultaneously is valuable, but recognising its limits prevents overestimating our ability to handle complex simultaneous tasks.
items.example: A nurse monitors a patient's vital signs on a screen while listening to a colleague relay information about medication, dividing attention between two clinically important inputs.

items.title: I can explain the role of selective attention as a filter for prioritising information
items.what: Selective attention acts as a filter that prioritises incoming information according to its importance, allowing us to focus on the most relevant stimuli and process them thoroughly enough to make sense of and use them.
items.why: Because we cannot attend to everything at once, selective attention ensures that the most useful, meaningful, or unexpected information receives our limited cognitive resources.
items.example: A driver ignores roadside advertising and pedestrians on the footpath to maintain full attention on the traffic conditions directly ahead.

items.title: I can explain the predictive principle of attentional allocation
items.what: The predictive principle states that we selectively attend to stimuli that are personally meaningful and important to us, even among many competing stimuli.
items.why: This principle explains why we notice things that matter to us, such as hearing our own name mentioned in a nearby conversation we were otherwise not listening to.
items.example: A psychology student notices references to memory research in a general science podcast because the topic is personally relevant to their current studies.

subtopic.why: Understanding how each type of attention serves a different function helps explain real-world behaviours like noticing a familiar name in a crowd, losing track of a task when fatigued, or being able to drive and hold a conversation.

items.title: I can explain the uncertainty principle of attentional allocation
items.what: The uncertainty principle states that attention is most strongly captured by stimuli that are unpredictable or unfamiliar, because such stimuli have the potential to carry important information about novel or dangerous consequences.
items.why: This principle has an evolutionary basis, helping individuals quickly detect and respond to unexpected threats or changes in the environment.
items.example: A student studying in a quiet library immediately notices and looks up when an unusual sound occurs, even though they were deeply focused on their work.

items.title: I can distinguish between sensation and perception
items.what: Sensation is the process of receiving and detecting raw sensory stimuli via sensory organs and sending this information to the brain as a neural impulse. Perception is the subsequent process of selecting, organising, and interpreting that sensory information to bring it into conscious awareness.
items.why: The two processes are sequential and distinct: sensation provides the raw data, while perception gives it meaning. Conflating them leads to incorrect explanations of how we experience the world.
items.example: The eye detects light reflecting off a stop sign (sensation), and the brain then interprets the red octagonal shape as a command to stop (perception).

subtopic.name: Sensation and Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can describe the three stages of perception: selection, organisation, and interpretation
items.what: Selection is the process of attending to certain stimuli and excluding others. Organisation involves regrouping the selected features into a coherent pattern. Interpretation assigns meaning to the organised information, drawing on memory, mood, and expectations.
items.why: Each stage transforms raw sensory data into a form the brain can consciously understand, and errors or influences at any stage can change what we ultimately perceive.
items.example: When seeing a smiley face drawn with simple lines: selection attends to the lines, organisation groups them into a face shape, and interpretation recognises it as expressing happiness.

subtopic.name: Sensation and Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can describe the pathway of visual sensation from the eye to the brain
items.what: Visual sensation begins when light enters the eye through the pupil and is focused by the lens onto the retina. Sensory receptors in the retina convert the light energy into a neural impulse, which is sent to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe for perceptual processing.
items.why: Understanding this pathway clarifies where in the process biological abnormalities (such as myopia or colour blindness) can alter what we see.
items.example: When a person looks at a green apple, light from the apple travels through the lens, hits the retina, is converted to a neural signal, and is processed in the occipital lobe.

subtopic.name: Sensation and Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can describe the pathway of gustatory sensation from the tongue to the brain
items.what: Gustatory sensation begins when saliva breaks food into tastants, which are detected by gustatory receptors within taste buds on the tongue and around the mouth. The signal is converted to a neural impulse and sent to the primary gustatory cortex in the parietal lobe.
items.why: Knowing the gustatory pathway explains how factors like reduced saliva production with age or fewer taste buds affect the intensity of flavour we perceive.
items.example: When eating a piece of dark chocolate, the bitter tastants are detected by gustatory receptors on the tongue and the neural signal travels to the parietal lobe for processing.

subtopic.name: Sensation and Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can name the five basic flavours detected by the gustatory system
items.what: The five basic flavours are sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami (savoury). These are the fundamental categories of taste that gustatory receptors are sensitive to, and complex flavour experiences are built from combinations of these.
items.why: Understanding the five basic flavours clarifies why removing one sensory input (such as smell) can reduce the richness of flavour perception even though the tastants themselves are unchanged.
items.example: Coffee is primarily bitter (one of the five basic flavours), which is why children with more taste buds tend to find it unpleasant, while adults with fewer taste buds may find it more tolerable.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the distinction between sensation and perception, the three stages of perception (selection, organisation, interpretation), and the specific sensory pathways and brain regions involved in visual and gustatory perception.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can explain how other senses contribute to gustatory perception
items.what: Gustatory perception is not limited to taste alone; the senses of smell, vision, and touch (texture) all contribute. The gustatory cortex integrates information from the olfactory cortex (smell) and the somatosensory cortex (texture) to form a complete perception of flavour.
items.why: This integration explains everyday experiences such as food tasting blander when you have a blocked nose, and why the colour or texture of food can change how its flavour is perceived.
items.example: When eating a strawberry, the sweet taste is combined with the fruity smell and soft texture to produce the full perception of strawberry flavour; blocking the nose reduces this richness.

subtopic.why: Distinguishing sensation from perception is fundamental to understanding how raw sensory data becomes conscious experience. This underpins explanations of why two people can detect the same stimulus but perceive it differently.

items.title: I can define bottom-up processing and explain when it is used
items.what: Bottom-up processing occurs when perception is built entirely from incoming sensory information, moving from specific stimulus details to a general understanding. It is typically used when the stimulus is unfamiliar or complex.
items.why: Bottom-up processing is the perceptual starting point for new experiences; it ensures that novel stimuli are analysed on their own terms rather than forced into a familiar category that may not fit.
items.example: A student learning Japanese for the first time reads each character individually, building up meaning letter by letter without being able to rely on prior recognition.

subtopic.name: Types of Perceptual Processing
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two contrasting types of perceptual processing: bottom-up processing, which is driven by incoming sensory data, and top-down processing, which is driven by prior knowledge, expectations, and schemas. It explains how both types operate and interact.
subtopic.why: Distinguishing bottom-up from top-down processing is central to explaining how the same sensory stimulus can be perceived differently by different people, and why familiarity speeds up recognition.

items.title: I can define top-down processing and explain when it is used
items.what: Top-down processing occurs when prior knowledge and expectations guide perception, moving from general knowledge to specific stimulus details. It is typically used when the stimulus is familiar and less complex.
items.why: Top-down processing makes perception faster and more efficient for routine stimuli, but it also introduces the possibility of misperception when expectations do not match reality.
items.example: A fluent reader can understand a sentence even if some letters are smudged or missing, because their prior knowledge of English fills in the gaps.

subtopic.why: Distinguishing bottom-up from top-down processing is central to explaining how the same sensory stimulus can be perceived differently by different people, and why familiarity speeds up recognition.

items.title: I can explain the role of schemas in top-down processing
items.what: Schemas are the collections of basic knowledge about a concept or stimulus stored in memory. In top-down processing, incoming stimuli are matched to existing schemas so they can be quickly recognised and interpreted.
items.why: Schemas make perception efficient, but they can also cause misperception when a stimulus is ambiguous and the wrong schema is applied.
items.example: A child who has only seen Labrador dogs may apply their dog schema to a fox when they first see one, perceiving it as a type of dog because it matches enough features of their existing schema.

subtopic.why: Distinguishing bottom-up from top-down processing is central to explaining how the same sensory stimulus can be perceived differently by different people, and why familiarity speeds up recognition.

items.title: I can compare bottom-up and top-down processing using direction and type of information
items.what: Bottom-up processing moves from specific stimulus features to general meaning, and is used for unfamiliar or complex stimuli. Top-down processing moves from general prior knowledge to specific features, and is used for familiar or less complex stimuli.
items.why: Being able to compare these two types of processing precisely, including their directions and contexts, is essential for correctly applying them to scenarios in exam questions.
items.example: Seeing a word written in an unusual font requires bottom-up processing to decode each letter; reading the same word in a familiar font activates top-down processing based on pattern recognition.

subtopic.why: Distinguishing bottom-up from top-down processing is central to explaining how the same sensory stimulus can be perceived differently by different people, and why familiarity speeds up recognition.

items.title: I can explain how bottom-up and top-down processing work together in one scenario
items.what: Both types of processing often occur together. Bottom-up processing registers the raw sensory details of a stimulus, while top-down processing draws on past experience to interpret those details. The two interact continuously during perception.
items.why: In real-world perception, stimuli are rarely processed by only one type; understanding their interaction explains how we can simultaneously notice new details and apply existing knowledge.
items.example: After stubbing a toe on a table leg (bottom-up: pain signals register the hazard), a person later perceives that table leg as dangerous and walks more carefully around it (top-down: past experience guides future perception).

items.title: I can describe the roles of rods and cones as photoreceptors in the retina
items.what: Rods are photoreceptors located mainly on the outer edges of the retina that allow vision in low light and enable peripheral vision but do not process colour or fine detail. Cones are concentrated in the fovea (centre of the retina) and are specialised for colour vision and fine detail in well-lit conditions.
items.why: The different functions of rods and cones explain many aspects of visual experience, including why colours appear washed out in dim light and why we see more clearly when looking directly at an object.
items.example: In a dark cinema, a person uses their rods to detect shapes and movement in their peripheral vision but cannot clearly make out the colour of their friend's jacket.

subtopic.name: Factors Influencing Visual Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the biological (photoreceptors, depth cues), psychological (Gestalt principles, visual constancies, perceptual set), and social (cultural norms) factors that influence what we see and how we interpret visual information.
subtopic.why: Visual perception is not a simple recording of reality; it is actively constructed by the brain and shaped by multiple interacting factors. This explains why individuals with different backgrounds, experiences, or biology can look at the same scene and perceive it differently.

items.title: I can explain colour blindness and myopia as biological abnormalities affecting visual perception
items.what: Colour blindness results from defective cones and affects approximately 8% of males and 0.5% of females, making it difficult to distinguish certain colours (red-green, blue-yellow, or all colours). Myopia (short-sightedness) results from refractory errors where the focal point falls in front of the retina, causing distant objects to appear blurry.
items.why: These conditions demonstrate that biological differences in the visual sensory system directly affect what an individual is able to perceive, independent of psychological or social influences.
items.example: A person with red-green colour blindness looking at a traffic light may struggle to distinguish the red stop light from the green go light based on colour alone.

items.title: I can distinguish between monocular and binocular depth cues
items.what: Monocular depth cues allow depth perception using only one eye and include accommodation, motion parallax, and pictorial depth cues. Binocular depth cues require both eyes and include retinal disparity and convergence.
items.why: Depth cues are the biological and perceptual mechanisms that allow us to perceive a three-dimensional world from a two-dimensional retinal image, which is essential for spatial navigation and object interaction.
items.example: A person who covers one eye can still judge that a nearby tree is closer than a distant mountain using monocular cues such as relative size, but loses the added depth precision provided by retinal disparity.

items.title: I can describe at least three pictorial depth cues and explain how each signals distance
items.what: Pictorial depth cues are monocular cues used in 2D art and real scenes. They include: relative size (smaller image equals greater distance), height in visual field (closer to the horizon equals further away), linear perspective (parallel lines converging in the distance), interposition (an overlapping object is closer), and texture gradient (more texture detail equals closer proximity).
items.why: Pictorial depth cues are psychological in nature because they are interpreted in the brain rather than derived purely from the eye, and they are the basis of how artists create the illusion of depth on a flat surface.
items.example: In a photograph of a long straight road, the white line markings appear to converge at the horizon (linear perspective), signalling that the far end of the road is distant.

items.title: I can explain retinal disparity and convergence as binocular depth cues
items.what: Retinal disparity refers to the slight difference between the images received by each eye due to their approximately 7 cm separation; the greater the disparity, the closer the object. Convergence refers to the inward turning of both eyes when focusing on a close object; the greater the muscular strain, the closer the object.
items.why: Both cues rely on the use of both eyes simultaneously, which is why people with vision in only one eye have reduced depth perception for objects at close range.
items.example: When holding a finger 10 cm from your nose and alternately closing each eye, the finger appears to jump position; this positional difference is retinal disparity, and the eye-muscle strain felt when both eyes focus on it is convergence.

items.title: I can describe the four Gestalt principles and explain how each organises visual stimuli
items.what: The four Gestalt principles are: proximity (items close together are grouped), similarity (items that look alike are grouped), figure-ground (some elements are seen as foreground, others as background), and closure (incomplete images are mentally completed into wholes). They apply automatically during the organisation stage of perception.
items.why: Gestalt principles explain how the brain creates coherent, meaningful images from fragmented visual signals, which is why we can recognise objects even when parts are hidden or the image is imperfect.
items.example: A student looks at a partially obscured road sign and mentally fills in the hidden letters to read the full word (closure), while perceiving the bold text as standing out against the coloured background (figure-ground).

subtopic.why: Visual perception is not a simple recording of reality; it is actively constructed by the brain and shaped by multiple interacting factors. This explains why individuals with different backgrounds, experiences, or biology can look at the same scene and perceive it differently.

items.title: I can explain visual constancies (shape, size, brightness) and how they maintain stable perception
items.what: Visual constancies are the ability to perceive objects as remaining the same despite changes in the retinal image. Shape constancy maintains perceived shape when viewing angle changes, size constancy maintains perceived size when distance changes, and brightness constancy maintains perceived colour/brightness when lighting changes.
items.why: Without constancies, every change in viewing angle, distance, or lighting would cause us to perceive objects as fundamentally altered, making the visual world chaotic and unstable.
items.example: A person walking away from you appears to cast a progressively smaller image on your retina, but size constancy means you perceive them as the same height moving further away, not as shrinking.

items.title: I can explain how perceptual set and historical experiences influence visual perception
items.what: A perceptual set is a predisposition to perceive certain features of sensory stimuli and ignore others, shaped by prior experiences, expectations, and schemas. Historical experiences create expectations about what is likely to appear in a given context, biasing both the selection and interpretation stages of perception.
items.why: Perceptual set illustrates how perception is not a neutral process; our history and expectations actively shape what we notice and how we interpret ambiguous stimuli.
items.example: A mechanic scanning a car engine quickly notices a misaligned part because their years of experience have created a perceptual set attuned to mechanical abnormalities that a non-mechanic would overlook.

items.title: I can explain how cultural norms act as a social factor influencing visual perception
items.what: Cultural norms are shared standards and values within a cultural group that shape what people attend to and how they interpret visual scenes. For example, research shows East Asian individuals tend to attend to the broad context of a scene, while Western individuals tend to focus on a prominent individual object within it.
items.why: Cultural differences in visual perception demonstrate that perception is not purely biological; the social environment in which a person develops shapes their perceptual habits in systematic, measurable ways.
items.example: When shown a photograph of a fish tank, Japanese participants tended to describe the background plants, water colour, and overall scene, while American participants focused on describing the largest, most colourful fish.

subtopic.name: Factors Influencing Visual Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the biological (photoreceptors, depth cues), psychological (Gestalt principles, visual constancies, perceptual set), and social (cultural norms) factors that influence what we see and how we interpret visual information.
subtopic.why: Visual perception is not a simple recording of reality; it is actively constructed by the brain and shaped by multiple interacting factors. This explains why individuals with different backgrounds, experiences, or biology can look at the same scene and perceive it differently.

items.title: I can explain how age acts as a biological factor that influences gustatory perception
items.what: As people age, the number of taste buds and gustatory receptors decreases, the papillae on the tongue become less sensitive, saliva production declines, and the sense of smell weakens. Together, these changes reduce the intensity of flavour perception.
items.why: Understanding age-related changes in gustatory perception explains why children are often fussier eaters than adults and why older adults may require stronger seasoning to perceive flavour at the same intensity as younger people.
items.example: A 70-year-old finding that the pie they loved at age 25 now tastes bland is likely experiencing an age-related reduction in gustatory receptor sensitivity rather than a change in the pie's recipe.

subtopic.name: Factors Influencing Gustatory Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the biological (age, genetics), psychological (appearance, food packaging, perceptual set), and social (culture) factors that influence how we perceive flavour. It builds on the mechanisms of gustatory sensation introduced in the sensation and perception subtopic.
subtopic.why: Flavour perception is not determined by taste alone; it is actively shaped by who we are, what we expect, and the cultural context in which we eat. This explains why the same food can taste very different to different people.

items.title: I can explain how genetics acts as a biological factor that influences gustatory perception
items.what: Genetic differences determine the number of taste buds a person inherits and their sensitivity to particular flavours. People can be classified as supertasters (highly sensitive, more taste buds), medium-tasters (average sensitivity), or non-tasters (lower sensitivity, fewer taste buds). Genetic factors also determine specific food preferences, such as whether coriander tastes pleasant or soapy.
items.why: Genetics explains why flavour preferences differ meaningfully between individuals even when they have had identical food experiences, highlighting a fundamental biological source of variation in gustatory perception.
items.example: A supertaster finds dark chocolate intensely bitter and unpleasant at 70% cocoa, while a non-taster with fewer taste buds finds the same chocolate mildly bitter and enjoyable.

items.title: I can explain how the appearance of food (colour and shape) influences gustatory perception
items.what: The colour and shape of food influence expectations about its flavour, which then shape actual perception. Colours that do not match expectations can cause people to misidentify flavours or perceive something as tasting wrong. Round shapes tend to be associated with sweetness, while angular shapes are associated with bitterness or savoury flavour.
items.why: The influence of appearance demonstrates that gustatory perception integrates information from the visual cortex, meaning what we see actively shapes what we taste.
items.example: When Cadbury changed their chocolate block from rectangular segments to rounded segments without altering the recipe, customers reported the chocolate tasted sweeter, consistent with the association between round shapes and sweetness.

items.title: I can explain how food packaging influences gustatory perception through perceptual set
items.what: Brand names, logos, images, and visual design on food packaging can influence expectations about flavour quality, freshness, or character. Familiarity with a trusted or expensive brand can lead people to perceive its products as tasting better, while packaging imagery (such as farming scenes on a juice bottle) can create associations with freshness.
items.why: Packaging effects show that gustatory perception can be altered before food is even tasted, revealing how strongly our perceptual set shapes sensory experience.
items.example: Children in a study reported that identical chips tasted better when served in a packaging they recognised as McDonald's compared to a plain white bag, demonstrating that brand recognition influenced their gustatory perception.

items.title: I can explain how perceptual set acts as a psychological factor influencing gustatory perception
items.what: A person's perceptual set for food is shaped by their historical experiences, mood, motivation, and contextual expectations. These factors prime the individual to expect certain flavours, making them more likely to perceive the flavour in line with those expectations, even if it does not fully match the actual sensory input.
items.why: Understanding perceptual set in gustatory perception explains why the context in which food is eaten can alter its perceived taste, and why our history with a food matters as much as the food's actual chemistry.
items.example: A person who has previously enjoyed a particular brand of coffee perceives a new batch from that brand as high quality before tasting it, and the positive expectation enhances their actual perception of its flavour.

items.title: I can explain how culture acts as a social factor influencing gustatory perception
items.what: The foods that are normal and familiar within a person's ethnic and social culture shape their taste preferences and their tolerance for unfamiliar flavours. Cultural values around health, socialising, or food traditions also influence how flavoursome or enjoyable food is perceived to be.
items.why: Cultural influences on taste demonstrate that gustatory perception is partly learned through social experience, which is why food preferences vary systematically across different cultural groups.
items.example: A person raised in a culture where spicy food is common from childhood perceives moderately spicy dishes as pleasant and normal, while someone from a culture with little spicy food tradition may perceive the same dish as uncomfortably intense.

items.title: I can evaluate the relative influence of biological, psychological, and social factors on gustatory perception in a given scenario
items.what: In any given scenario involving taste, multiple factors may interact simultaneously. A complete evaluation identifies which factor is most relevant, justifies why, and acknowledges how other factors may also be contributing.
items.why: Real-world gustatory experiences are rarely explained by a single factor alone; the ability to identify and weigh multiple influences is essential for complex exam-style analysis questions.
items.example: A supertaster (biological) from a health-conscious culture (social) who sees fresh produce images on a smoothie label (psychological) will have their gustatory perception shaped by all three factors at once, though the biological sensitivity may most strongly determine the intensity of what they taste.
